name: Mandaeism
info: Mandaeism is a Gnostic, monotheistic and ethnic religion of the Mandaeans, centred on the Great Life, Hayyi Rabbi, and on John the Baptist, practised mainly in southern Iraq and Khuzestan and known for its frequent baptisms in flowing water.

facts.origin: According to the Haran Gawaita, Nasoraean disciples of John the Baptist left Jerusalem in the first century CE and settled in southern Mesopotamia; scholars dispute whether the origin lay in Israel or in Mesopotamia.
facts.founder: none: Mandaeans hold Adam to be the founder of the religion and John the Baptist its greatest and final prophet, who renews and reforms an ancient faith; they do not regard John as its founder.
facts.scriptures: The Ginza Rabba (Left and Right Ginza), the Qulasta prayerbook, the Draša d-Yahya or Book of John, the Haran Gawaita, the Diwan Abatur and the Book of the Zodiac, in Mandaic.
facts.followers: Between 60,000 and 100,000 worldwide; 60,000 to 70,000 in 2007, when about 5,000 remained in Iraq; around 10,000 in Australia.

t: Mandaeans believe in one God, Hayyi Rabbi, the Great Life, whose symbol is living water, and for that reason they need to live near rivers; baptism in flowing water is performed every Sunday.
Mandaeans revere Adam, Seth, Noah, Shem and above all John the Baptist, whom they hold to be the greatest and final prophet, and they regard Jesus as a false prophet.
Mandaeism does not allow conversion, and the community has shrunk in Iraq: by 2007 about 5,000 Mandaeans remained there, as many fled the turmoil that followed the invasion of 2003.
dyk: Mandaeans call every river fit for baptism Yardena, after the River Jordan, and every mandi, their place of worship, must stand beside a river or, in modern buildings, hold a bath in its place.

sections.origins:
Mandaeism, called mandaiuta in Classical Mandaic and sometimes Nasoraeanism, is the religion of the Mandaeans, who take their name from manda, “knowledge”. Their account of their early history is the Haran Gawaita, written between the 4th and 6th centuries. It tells that Nasoraean Mandaeans, disciples of John the Baptist, left Jerusalem in the first century CE, reportedly because of persecution, and went to Haran or Hauran, then to the Median hills in Iran, and finally settled in southern Mesopotamia. Many specialists, including Jorunn Jacobsen Buckley, accept this account. Mandaeans themselves hold that their religion predates Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

Scholars disagree. Kurt Rudolph, Mark Lidzbarski, Rudolf Macúch, E. S. Drower, James F. McGrath, Charles G. Häberl and others argue for an Israelite origin, and most of them see a historical link with John the Baptist’s inner circle. Edmondo Lupieri holds that Mandaeism is a post-Christian Gnostic offshoot in southern Mesopotamia and names Zazai d-Gawazta as its founder in the second century; Buckley answers that scribes older than Zazai copied the Ginza Rabba. Christa Müller-Kessler also argues for a Mesopotamian origin, Edwin Yamauchi for one in the Transjordan with a later merging with Mesopotamian beliefs, and Kevin van Bladel for a date no earlier than the fifth century in Sasanian Mesopotamia, a thesis James F. McGrath has criticised. The Mandaean priest and scholar Brikha Nasoraia accepts two lines of descent, one from the Jordan valley and one native to southern Mesopotamia.
sections.beliefs:
Mandaeans believe in one God, most often called Hayyi Rabbi, “The Great Life”, whose symbol is living water (Yardena); other names include Mare d’Rabuta, “Lord of Greatness”, Malka d-Nhura, “King of Light”, and Hayyi Qadmaiyi, “The First Life”. They hold that God has no partner and that the world arose by emanation. Many uthras, angels or guardians, come from the light and praise God; among them Manda d-Hayyi brings knowledge to the earth and Hibil Ziwa conquers the World of Darkness. Ptahil, the “Fourth Life”, creates the material world with the help of the evil spirit Ruha, so that the world is a mixture of light and dark, and Abatur, the “Third Life”, weighs the souls of the dead. According to E. S. Drower, the Mandaean gnosis is marked by a supreme formless Entity, dualism, the soul as an exile whose home is that Entity, saviour spirits and mysteries or sacraments that aid the soul’s rebirth in a spiritual body.

Mandaeans hold the soul to be immortal, with reward and punishment in the next life but no eternal punishment, since God is merciful. They recognise Adam, Seth, Noah, Shem and John the Baptist as prophets, John being the greatest and final; they do not count Abraham, Moses or Jesus as Mandaean prophets and consider Jesus a false prophet. Their teaching is pacifist, and they place a high priority on family life. They abstain from strong drink and most red meat, and they forbid circumcision, holding that the creator made the human body complete. Sunday is their holy day.
sections.texts:
The most important Mandaean scripture is the Ginza Rabba, a collection of history, theology and prayers in two halves, the Left Ginza and the Right Ginza. From the colophons of the Left Ginza, Jorunn J. Buckley has identified an unbroken chain of copyists back to the late second or early third century, which attests Mandaeans in the late Parthian Empire. The Qulasta is the canonical prayerbook; the Draša d-Yahya, the Mandaean Book of John, is open to laymen and initiates alike and includes a dialogue between John and Jesus; the Haran Gawaita tells the community’s history; the Diwan Abatur describes the regions through which the soul ascends.

The oldest Mandaean texts are lead amulets from about the third century CE, followed by incantation bowls from about 600 CE. The main religious texts survive in manuscripts no older than the sixteenth century, most from the eighteenth and nineteenth, and they may have been passed on orally before scribes wrote them down, which makes dating and authorship difficult. The language is Mandaic, an Eastern Aramaic language written in a cursive variant of the Parthian chancellery script; many laypeople do not speak it, though some Mandaeans in Iran and Iraq speak Neo-Mandaic. Because the Mandaeans have remained separate and intensely private, reports of them have come mainly from outsiders such as the Orientalist Julius Heinrich Petermann, the French vice-consul Nicolas Siouffi and the anthropologist Lady E. S. Drower.
sections.spread:
The religion has been practised mainly around the lower Karun, Euphrates and Tigris and the rivers of the Shatt al-Arab, in southern Iraq and Khuzestan in Iran. Under Parthian rule the Mandaeans flourished under royal protection, which ended when Bahram I became Sasanian emperor and his high priest Kartir persecuted all non-Zoroastrians. At the start of the Muslim conquest of Mesopotamia, in about 640, their leader Anush bar Danqa is said to have shown the Ginza Rabba to the Muslim authorities and so had Mandaeans counted among the People of the Book; the account is likely apocryphal, since it has him travel to Baghdad, founded in 762.

At some point the Mandaeans were identified with the Sabians whom the Quran names beside Jews, Christians and Zoroastrians. The earliest source to say so unambiguously is Ḥasan bar Bahlul (fl. 950–1000), citing the Abbasid vizier ibn Muqla, and it is not clear whether the Mandaeans of that period already called themselves Sabians. Around 1290 the Dominican Riccoldo da Monte di Croce met them in Mesopotamia, and in the 16th and 17th centuries members of the Discalced Carmelite mission in Basra called them “Christians of Saint John”, a name that has been judged a misnomer, since Mandaeans consider Jesus a false prophet.

Until the Iraq War almost all Mandaeans lived in Iraq. Many have fled since the invasion of 2003 and the related rise in sectarian violence by extremists, most of them to Iran, Syria and Jordan, and others to Sweden, the Netherlands, Germany, the United States, Canada, New Zealand, the UK and above all Australia.
sections.community:
Mandaean society draws a strict line between laity and priests. In E. S. Drower’s account the laity are Mandaeans, “gnostics”, while a man who becomes a priest enters the priesthood, tarmiduta, and true enlightenment, Nasiruta, is reserved for a very few. There are three grades of priest: the tarmidia, “disciples”, the ganzibria, “treasurers”, and the rišama, “leader of the people”. The present priesthood traces its immediate origin to the first half of the nineteenth century: cholera at Shushtar in Iran in 1831 destroyed most of the Mandaean religious authorities there, and two surviving acolytes, Yahia Bihram and Ram Zihrun, reestablished the priesthood at Suq al-Shuyukh. There were two dozen priests in the world in 2009, and their number has since been growing.

The two chief ceremonies are baptism, the masbuta, and the masiqta, a ritual meal in memory of the dead that is believed to help souls on their way to the World of Light. Baptism is performed every Sunday, usually by full immersion in flowing water, and is followed by anointing with sesame oil and a communion of bread and water. Mandaeans also wash before prayer, pray three times a day facing north, and give alms. A place of worship, the mandi, stands beside a river and carries the drabsha, a banner of olive wood and white silk with seven myrtle branches. Mandaean tradition forbids revealing the names of the angels to a gentile. Polygyny is accepted but uncommon. Mandaeism does not allow conversion, and the status of Mandaeans who marry outside the faith, and of their children, is disputed.
sections.legacy:
Scholars have long compared Mandaeism with other traditions of late antiquity. Early Mandaean concepts and terms recur in the Dead Sea Scrolls, and Mandaean practices resemble those the Essenes and the Hemerobaptists are reported to have followed, among them frequent baptism and north–south graves. Kurt Rudolph has noted parallels with the Sethian texts of Nag Hammadi, and a Mandaean baptismal formula was adopted by Valentinian Gnostics in the second century CE. E. S. Drower held that the earliest Manichaean psalms were paraphrases or translations of Mandaic originals, while Jorunn J. Buckley suggests that the Mandaeans may have helped to develop Gnosticism. Nathaniel Deutsch writes that Mandaeans and Jews in Babylonia shared magical and angelological traditions, so that Mandaean uthra names appear in Jewish magic texts, though it cannot be said in which direction influence ran.

Today the community is estimated at 60,000 to 100,000 people. Iran’s Mandaeans have been put at between 5,000 and at most 10,000 in one article of 2009, and at as many as 60,000 by Al Arabiya in 2011. Around 10,000 live in Australia, mainly around Sydney, about 15% of the world total, and about 2,500 in Jordan. The United States gave Iranian Mandaeans protective refugee status in 2002 and Iraqi Mandaeans in 2007; a community of about 2,500, mostly from Iraq, has lived in Worcester, Massachusetts, since 2008.

summary: Mandaeism is the Gnostic, monotheistic and ethnic religion of the Mandaeans, who revere John the Baptist and worship the Great Life, Hayyi Rabbi, with weekly baptism in flowing water. Long centred on southern Iraq and Khuzestan, the community has shrunk in Iraq since 2003 and now lives largely in diaspora, above all in Australia.
references: Jorunn J. Buckley, The Mandaeans: Ancient Texts and Modern People (Oxford University Press, 2002)
Ethel Stephana Drower, The Mandaeans of Iraq and Iran: Their Cults, Customs, Magic Legends, and Folklore (Clarendon Press, 1937)
Edmondo Lupieri, The Mandaeans: The Last Gnostics (Eerdmans, 2001)
Kevin van Bladel, From Sasanian Mandaeans to Ṣābians of the Marshes (Brill, 2017)
notes: Start 100 (circa): the Haran Gawaita dates the migration to the first century CE; scholars dispute whether the religion arose in Israel or Mesopotamia, and some date it later (Lupieri: second century; van Bladel: fifth century at the earliest). The oldest evidence is the colophon chain (late second or early third century) and lead amulets (c. third century).

Conflicting figures kept as the article gives them: 60,000 to 70,000 worldwide in 2007 (lede) against 60,000 to 100,000 (Demographics); Iran 5,000 to 10,000 (2009) against up to 60,000 (2011). Both are in the profile with their sources.

Left out: the article's long comparison sections on the Elkesaites, Bana'im, Maghariya and Samaritan Baptist sects, except as the legacy section summarises; the Epiphanius quotations; the claim that Abraham and Jesus were originally Mandaean priests.

Persecution: the article names the Sasanian persecution under Bahram I and Kartir (no date given) and the flight from Iraq after 2003; it gives no figures of killings, so none appear. Shlama Beth Qidra is dated by the article to the second century CE.
The article contradicts itself slightly on the Ginza Rabba's external links (a book titled Ginza Rabba is the Qolasta): not used. Event 2008 is the article's date for settlement in Worcester.
Event 'c. 950' uses fl. 950–1000 for al-Hasan ibn Bahlul; ibn Muqla lived c. 885–940.
